question: How many zones does the game normally use, and which of them belong to one player rather than being shared by everyone?
Is a player's library a hidden zone or a public one, and can a player look through or rearrange the order of their own library whenever they like?
Are cards a player has exiled public information by default, or can a player keep them secret?
When a permanent is destroyed and moves from the battlefield to the graveyard, is it still the same game object it was on the battlefield, or does something change about its identity?
If an effect would put an instant or sorcery card onto the battlefield, what actually happens to it?
If a token is moved off the battlefield (to a hand, graveyard, exile, or anywhere else), what happens to it, and can it ever come back?
Can players freely rearrange the order of objects on the stack, the way they might rearrange permanents on the battlefield?
Does every turn always include all five phases (beginning, precombat main, combat, postcombat main, ending), even if nothing happens during some of them?
In a two-player game, does the player who takes the very first turn get a draw step on that turn?

In a free-for-all multiplayer game with three or more players (not Two-Headed Giant), does the starting player skip the draw step of their first turn the way a starting player would in a two-player game?

In a Two-Headed Giant game, does the team that takes the first turn skip its draw step, and if a step isn't skipped, does each player on a team normally draw their own card during that team's draw step?
If a player is given several extra turns at once by different effects, in what order are those extra turns actually taken?
If an effect would cause a player to skip their next upkeep, but their upkeep has already started by the time that effect resolves, does the upkeep get retroactively skipped?
If several triggered abilities controlled by different players all trigger from the same event, in what order are they put on the stack?

Because the active player's simultaneously-triggered abilities are placed on the stack before a nonactive player's, does that mean the active player's version of the trigger actually resolves first or last relative to the nonactive player's?
Do static abilities ever get put on the stack the way triggered and activated abilities do?
If a targeted spell or ability is about to resolve and every single one of its targets has become illegal, what happens to it?
If a spell has two targets and only one of them becomes illegal before it resolves, does the whole spell fail, or does it still resolve and just skip the illegal target?
If an effect lets a player "choose new targets" for a spell or ability, must every one of the original targets actually be replaced?
If an effect lets a player "change the target(s)" of a spell (as opposed to "choose new targets"), can they change a target to something that isn't a legal target for that spell?
Can a spell or ability on the stack ever legally target itself?

If a spell or ability requires targets but its wording lets the caster choose any number of them, is choosing zero targets a legal choice, and if zero are chosen, is that spell or ability still considered "targeted"?
What single word most commonly marks an effect as a replacement effect rather than some other kind of continuous effect?
Can a replacement effect be created (by casting a spell or activating an ability) after the event it's meant to replace has already happened, and still change that outcome?

If a permanent has an effect like "if a creature you control would deal damage to a player, it deals double that damage instead," does that replacement effect apply once, or does it keep reapplying to its own already-doubled result?
If a source would deal 0 damage, and an effect says damage from that source would instead be increased or redirected, does that replacement effect do anything?
Is regeneration a triggered ability that goes on the stack, or is it a replacement effect?
Is an effect that tells a player to "skip" a step, phase, or turn a replacement effect, or some other kind of effect?

Are self-replacement effects (where part of a resolving spell's own effect replaces the rest of that same effect) continuous effects that exist independently on the battlefield, the same way most replacement effects do?
When one permanent becomes a copy of another, does it also copy the counters, marked damage, and other continuous effects that happened to be affecting the original at that moment?
If a token enters the battlefield as a copy of a permanent that has an enters-the-battlefield triggered ability, does that trigger actually fire for the token?
If permanent B has already become a copy of permanent A, and permanent A's copiable characteristics change afterward, does permanent B automatically update to match?
If an effect creates a copy of a spell that's on the stack, is that copy considered to have been "cast," the way the original spell was?
If a permanent spell (one that's still on the stack) is itself a copy of another permanent spell, what does it turn into as it resolves and moves to the battlefield?
If an object has a pair of linked abilities (where one ability refers only to things the other one did), and that object is copied, do the two abilities stay linked to each other on the copy?
What makes a game a "multiplayer game" under the rules -- is it about how many players began the game, or how many are still in it right now?
In a multiplayer game played between teams, who counts as a given player's opponents?
If a spell or ability uses the phrase "your team," and the game in question isn't a multiplayer team game, who does "your team" actually refer to?
What is each team's starting life total in a Two-Headed Giant game?
What is each player's starting life total in a Commander game?
When a player leaves a multiplayer game (for example, by losing), what happens to the objects that player owns?
If an effect would change control of an object to a player who has already left a multiplayer game, does that control change actually happen?
If a triggered ability would be controlled by a player who has already left a multiplayer game, does it get put on the stack?
In a multiplayer game, does the very first mulligan a player takes count toward how many cards they'll have to put on the bottom of their library, the way it would in a two-player game?
Does the multiplayer "free first mulligan" rule apply in a two-player Commander game?
Under the limited range of influence option, can a player's creature attack an opponent who is outside that player's range of influence?

In a Two-Headed Giant game (which uses the shared team turns option), does each player on the active team draw their own card during the team's shared draw step, or is there just one draw for the whole team?

If a player leaves a multiplayer game (for example, by losing) while they control a permanent with a leaves-the-battlefield triggered ability, does that ability actually trigger as the permanent leaves the game?

In a Two-Headed Giant game, if both teammates would draw from an empty library on the same shared draw step, but one of them has a replacement effect that replaces their draw with "win the game instead," does the other teammate's empty-library draw cause the team to lose before that win effect can be applied?

If a game-restarting effect ends a multiplayer game and starts a new one, and one of the original players had already left the game (lost) before the restart happened, is that departed player included in the new game?
Does activating a mana ability use up a player's priority the way casting a spell would, or can the same player still act again immediately afterward?
If a game begins with four players and drops down to two remaining players over the course of play, does it stop being a "multiplayer game" for rules purposes once only two players are left?

If two different players each control a separate instance of the same triggered ability, and both instances trigger off the same shared event, is it guaranteed that one specific player's version resolves before the other's, or could either one happen first depending on choices made?
When a spell is cast in response to another spell already on the stack, which one actually resolves first?

If an object checks whether a spell or ability "targets only" a single object or player, does it matter how many separate instances of the word "target" that spell used to point at the same object, or does it only care that a single distinct object/player was chosen overall?

If a permanent's activated ability has a restriction like "activate only once each turn," and that permanent is then copied by a fresh copy effect after the ability has already been used up for the turn, does the new copy inherit the used-up restriction, or does it start the turn fresh?
